title: a table, bread, wine, remember me
hook: a table, bread, wine, remember me

segments.voice: Yesterday, silence. Not the wind, not the earthquake, not the fire. A still small voice. Your line: quiet is where he is. Did you find your one quiet minute? Day nineteen.

The last dinner before someone moved away. A holiday table the week after a funeral. Years later, the menu is gone. What stays is who was there, and what somebody said. An upstairs room in Jerusalem, at Passover. Jesus and the twelve, at one table. He has just told them that one of them will betray him. And instead of a speech, he picks up the bread. That's the last supper. What he did with the bread and the cup, churches still do, in cathedrals and in kitchens, with the same few words. Today's word is that meal.
screen: `WHO WAS THERE. WHAT WAS SAID.` → `AN UPSTAIRS ROOM. PASSOVER.` → `HE PICKS UP THE BREAD.`

segments.voice: Communion. Here's a surprise first: the words Christians repeat at that table aren't only in the Gospels. They're in a letter too, and the letter may be older than any Gospel. Paul, writing to the church in Corinth, passes on what he says he had received and already handed on to them. In the old King James Bible: "the Lord Jesus the same night in which he was betrayed took bread: And when he had given thanks, he brake it, and said, Take, eat: this is my body, which is broken for you: this do in remembrance of me." Then the cup, and the same words again: in remembrance of me. The Greek word for remembrance is anamnesis. Christians often hear more in it than a memory in your head: a remembering you do, with your hands, so the thing is present again. Families do this at every holiday table. Jews do it at Passover, telling the story as if they'd been there. That was the meal Jesus was eating. The meal has several names. Communion, from a word Paul uses for sharing: all of us, one loaf. The Eucharist, from the Greek for giving thanks, because that's what he did first. The Lord's Supper. The Mass. And here's where Christians honestly differ, so here's who says what. Catholic and Orthodox Christians believe Christ is truly present in the bread and the wine. Not a symbol. Him. Some Protestant churches understand the meal as a memorial: the bread and wine are signs, and the remembering is the heart of it. Lutherans, Anglicans and Reformed churches each have their own careful words for how Christ is present in the meal. Churches have argued about this for centuries, and they still do. What they share is the shape of it: a table, bread, a cup, and the words, remember me.
screen: `THE WORDS ARE IN A LETTER TOO.` · `ANAMNESIS — REMEMBERING YOU DO.` · `COMMUNION. EUCHARIST. THE MASS.` · `WHO BELIEVES WHAT.` · then, large: `A MEAL IS A MEMORY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Seventy-five seconds. Sit, and breathe. Bring to mind a table from your life, with people around it. Maybe it's this week's. Maybe it's one from long ago. Picture who was there. Picture their hands, passing something. Hear one thing somebody said. Let yourself remember them, not just think about them. If you pray, you can hold those people in your prayer, the way this meal holds someone. If you don't, just let the table be full again for a minute. The bell holds the time.
Communion. Sharing one loaf and one cup. A meal that is a memory. Nineteenth word.
Your line: a meal is a memory. Today, eat one meal slowly. And if you're eating with someone, put your phone away and remember that this one counts too. Day nineteen.

howItsDone: Christians share communion with bread and wine (or grape juice), as Jesus did at the last supper. Catholic and Orthodox churches celebrate it at every Mass or Divine Liturgy; Protestant churches share it weekly, monthly or a few times a year; and a few groups, such as Quakers, keep no outward meal.

original.note: Greek. remembrance, remembering. "this do in remembrance of me" (Luke 22:19; 1 Corinthians 11:24).

trapdoor: what you thought: a small bit of bread and a sip in church.
what it means: the meal Jesus gave on the night he was betrayed, which Christians repeat, remembering him.
what a scholar hears: Paul's account in 1 Corinthians 11 may be older than any Gospel. and anamnesis is a remembering you act out, not just recall.

notes: Review 2026-10-01: hook rewritten (no 'Think of'/'Now picture'; 'thirteen men' to Jesus and the twelve; dropped 'every week for two thousand years'); 'about twenty years later' and 'oldest account' softened to 'may be older than any Gospel'; anamnesis gloss framed as how Christians hear it; Protestant/Lutheran/Anglican/Reformed views reworded so Lutherans are not placed 'in between'; 'what they all do' cut (Quakers and some others keep no outward meal); games and howItsDone aligned.

Beliefs about the Eucharist are summarized briefly (Catholic and Orthodox: real presence; many Protestants: memorial; Lutherans, Anglicans and others in between). Reformed Christians (e.g. Calvin's spiritual presence) are folded into 'many others'. Please check each group would recognize itself; the memorial wording especially.
1 Corinthians dated about twenty years after the crucifixion (c. AD 53–55) and before the Gospels: the common scholarly view; confirm wording.
'Communion' from Paul's word koinonia (1 Cor 10:16, 'the communion of the body of Christ'): stated as 'a word Paul uses for sharing'.
John's Gospel sets the supper just before Passover; the Synoptics make it a Passover meal. The script follows the Synoptic setting ('at Passover'); a Keeper may want a hedge.
Grape juice mentioned in howItsDone for churches that use it.
